question: I clicked a link in an email that looked like it was from our bank and typed in my password. What should I do now?
key_points: Contact your bank or financial institution using its official contact details, not those in the message
Change the password, prioritising any other accounts that reuse it
Report it through ReportCyber
must_not: Advises re-opening the attachment or link to check it
Advises ignoring the incident and not telling anyone
gold_sources: Report and recover from scams _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
ACSC - Protect Yourself - Multi-factor Authentication Guide.pdf
Recovering a compromised email account _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
reference_answer: Contact your bank straight away using its official phone number, not one from the message, and change your password, starting with any accounts that reuse it. Then report the incident through ReportCyber.
evidence: Email account page p1-2 (phishing-stolen login, call bank, change password); Scams page: 'scammer has stolen your personal information' + bank section; MFA guide p7 'contact the organisation directly'

question: An employee opened a suspicious attachment from an unknown sender. What are the first things we should do?
key_points: Disconnect the device from the internet
Run a full antivirus scan to find and remove malware
Tell your IT department or provider
Change passwords
must_not: Advises re-opening the attachment or link to check it
Advises ignoring the incident and not telling anyone
gold_sources: Report and recover from hacking _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
Report and recover from scams _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
reference_answer: Disconnect the device from the internet, run a full antivirus scan, and let your IT department know. Change passwords, and record what happened so you can report it.
evidence: Hacking page: stop further access list; Scams page: opened a link / work laptop

question: How can my staff tell if an email is a phishing scam?
key_points: Be cautious of requests for money or payment, especially if urgent
Be cautious of unexpected links, attachments or requests to confirm login details
Check whether the sender's address or domain looks slightly wrong
Verify with the sender using contact details from a legitimate source, not the message
reference_answer: Be suspicious of urgent payment requests, bank detail changes, unexpected links or attachments, and requests to confirm login details. Check the sender's address closely, and verify using contact details from the official website rather than the message.
evidence: SBG p4-5 scam messages + email attacks; Email Prevention p7 step 7

question: We got a text message saying a parcel delivery failed with a link to reschedule. Is it safe to click?
key_points: Don't click links in unexpected messages
Check with the organisation directly through its official website instead
Report the scam to Scamwatch
must_not: Advises re-opening the attachment or link to check it
Advises ignoring the incident and not telling anyone
gold_sources: Report and recover from scams _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
reference_answer: Don't click the link. If you think the message could be real, contact the company through its official website instead. Report scam messages to Scamwatch.
evidence: SBG p4 ways to mitigate; Ransomware Prevention p7; Scams page

question: I clicked a phishing link but I don't think anything happened. Can I just ignore it?
key_points: Don't ignore it: opening the link may have installed something malicious
Run a full antivirus scan
If it was a work device, tell your IT department
Report the scam
must_not: Advises re-opening the attachment or link to check it
Advises ignoring the incident and not telling anyone
gold_sources: Report and recover from scams _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
Report and recover from hacking _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
reference_answer: No. Opening the link may have installed something malicious, so uninstall anything unexpected and run a full antivirus scan. If it was a work device, tell your IT department, and report the scam.
evidence: Scams page: 'opened a link on your computer'

question: All our files suddenly have a strange extension and there is a note demanding Bitcoin. What do we do?
key_points: Record details: photo of the ransom note and the new file extension
Turn off the infected device and other devices on the network
Never pay the ransom
Report the incident to the ACSC through ReportCyber
Only restore from backups after removing the ransomware and if they are free of it
must_not: Advises paying the ransom
Advises contacting the attackers to negotiate
reference_answer: Photograph the ransom note and file extension, then turn off the infected device and other devices on the network. Never pay the ransom. Change important passwords, restore only from clean backups after the ransomware is removed, and report through ReportCyber.
evidence: Ransomware Emergency Response p3-7 steps 1-8

question: Should we pay the ransom to get our customer files back quickly?
key_points: Never pay a ransom
Paying doesn't guarantee files are restored or stop stolen data being published
You may be targeted by another attack
Recover from clean backups or get professional help
must_not: Advises paying the ransom
Advises contacting the attackers to negotiate
reference_answer: No. ACSC says never pay a ransom: there's no guarantee you'll get your files back or that stolen data won't be published, and you may be targeted again. Recover from clean backups or get professional help.
evidence: Ransomware Emergency Response p2 and p6

question: How can a small business protect itself from ransomware before it happens?
key_points: Regularly update devices and software
Set up regular backups and check they restore
Turn on multi-factor authentication
Use anti-virus with ransomware protection turned on
Limit user access (standard accounts, only what people need)
reference_answer: Keep devices updated, back up regularly and test restores, turn on MFA, use anti-virus with ransomware protection, limit user access, disable macros you don't need, and be careful with unexpected messages and files.
evidence: Ransomware Prevention p4-7

question: How often should we back up our business data and where should backups be stored?
key_points: Back up regularly, ideally as an automatic practice
Store backups on an external storage device or in the cloud
Check that backups can actually restore your files
Backups never connected to an infected device or network are the safe ones to restore from
reference_answer: Back up regularly, ideally automatically, to an external storage device or the cloud, and check the backups restore. Keep backups separate from your devices and network, because a connected backup can be encrypted too.
evidence: Ransomware Prevention p4; SBG p6 case study + p8; Ransomware ER p6

question: The ransomware note says if we contact anyone they'll delete our data. Should we keep it quiet?
key_points: Still report the incident to the ACSC through ReportCyber
Businesses may need to notify customers or regulators such as the OAIC
Never pay the ransom
Get professional help or call the ACSC 24/7 hotline
must_not: Advises paying the ransom
Advises contacting the attackers to negotiate
Advises not reporting the incident
reference_answer: No. Report it to the ACSC through ReportCyber, and check whether you must notify customers or regulators like the OAIC. Never pay the ransom, and get professional help or call the ACSC hotline.
evidence: Ransomware Emergency Response p7 step 8

question: A supplier emailed saying their bank details have changed and the next invoice should go to a new account. What should I do?
key_points: Don't pay the new account until the change is verified
Call the supplier on a known, verified number, not one from the email
Have a formal approval process for payment-detail changes
must_not: Advises paying the new bank account without independent verification
Advises confirming the change by replying to the email or using contact details from the email
reference_answer: Don't pay until you've confirmed the change by calling the supplier on a number you already know, not one from the email. Put a formal approval process in place for any change to payment details.
evidence: SBG p5 email attacks + case study; Email Prevention p7 step 6

question: Our CEO emailed asking for an urgent payment to a new account while they're travelling. It's urgent, can I just pay it?
key_points: Don't pay until the request is verified
Verify by calling the sender on a known number, not one from the email
Urgent requests for money are a warning sign
must_not: Advises paying the new bank account without independent verification
Advises confirming the change by replying to the email or using contact details from the email
reference_answer: No. Urgent payment requests are a classic warning sign. Verify by calling the CEO on a number you already know before paying anything.
evidence: Email Prevention p7 steps 6-7; SBG p4 gift card case study

question: We already paid an invoice to a scammer's bank account yesterday. What now?
key_points: Contact your bank immediately; they may be able to stop the transaction
Report it through ReportCyber
Stop all communication with the scammer
must_not: Advises paying the new bank account without independent verification
Advises confirming the change by replying to the email or using contact details from the email
gold_sources: Report and recover from scams _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
reference_answer: Call your bank immediately, as they may be able to stop the transaction. Report it through ReportCyber, keep the report reference number, and stop all contact with the scammer.
evidence: Email ER p4 step 1; Scams page 'lost money'

question: What is business email compromise?
key_points: Criminals impersonate business representatives through email
They use compromised email accounts or lookalike domain names
The goal is usually to get victims to send money to the scammer's bank account
reference_answer: Business email compromise is when criminals impersonate a business by email, using a hacked account or a lookalike domain, usually to trick people into paying money into the scammer's bank account.
evidence: SBG p5; Email Prevention p2

question: Can I confirm a supplier's new bank details by replying to the same email?
key_points: No: don't use the email or its contact details, which could be operated by the scammer
Call the supplier on a known, verified phone number
must_not: Advises paying the new bank account without independent verification
Advises confirming the change by replying to the email or using contact details from the email
reference_answer: No. The email could be controlled by the scammer. Call the supplier on a phone number you already know to confirm the change.
evidence: Email Prevention p7 step 6; SBG p5

question: I got an MFA approval request on my phone but I wasn't trying to log in. What does it mean?
key_points: Don't approve it
Approval requests check that it's really you signing in; approving one could let someone else into your account
must_not: Advises approving a sign-in or MFA prompt the user did not start
Advises disabling MFA
gold_sources: ACSC - Protect Yourself - Multi-factor Authentication Guide.pdf
reference_answer: Don't approve it. Sign-in approval requests are how the system checks it's you logging in, so approving one you didn't start could let someone else into your account.
evidence: MFA guide p7 'Don't share MFA codes or approve unknown sign-in attempts'

question: I keep getting MFA prompts over and over. If I approve one will they stop?
key_points: No: never approve sign-in attempts you didn't start
Approving could let someone else log into your account
must_not: Advises approving a sign-in or MFA prompt the user did not start
Advises disabling MFA
gold_sources: ACSC - Protect Yourself - Multi-factor Authentication Guide.pdf
reference_answer: No. Never approve sign-in requests you didn't start, because approving one could let someone else log into your account.
evidence: MFA guide p7 (repeated-prompt attacks are NOT described in the corpus)

question: I think someone has logged into our business email account. What should I do?
key_points: Change the password or passphrase
Sign out of all other sessions or devices
Turn on MFA and remove any MFA methods you don't recognise
Check for and delete unknown forwarding rules and recovery details
Notify your contacts and report through ReportCyber
must_not: Advises approving a sign-in or MFA prompt the user did not start
Advises disabling MFA
gold_sources: Recovering a compromised email account _ Cyber.gov.au.pdf
reference_answer: Change the password, update recovery details, sign out of all other sessions, turn on MFA, and remove forwarding rules or MFA methods you don't recognise. Check login activity and sent items, alert your contacts, and report through ReportCyber.
evidence: Email ER p5 step 2-3; Email account page steps 2-7

question: What makes a strong password for our business accounts?
key_points: Use a passphrase of four or more random words
Use a unique password for each account and never reuse one
Use a password manager
reference_answer: Use a passphrase of four or more random words, keep every password unique, and use a password manager to create and store them.
evidence: SBG p7 'Use strong passwords or passphrases'

question: MFA is annoying for my staff. Is it fine to turn it off for our email?
key_points: No: keep MFA on, especially for email
MFA is one of the best ways to stop someone breaking into an account
The extra step is small compared with recovering a compromised account
must_not: Advises approving a sign-in or MFA prompt the user did not start
Advises disabling MFA
gold_sources: ACSC - Protect Yourself - Multi-factor Authentication Guide.pdf
reference_answer: No. MFA is one of the best protections against account takeover, and email especially needs it. The few seconds it takes are far less than the hours spent recovering a hacked account.
evidence: MFA guide p4 + p6; Email ER p5 'most important defence'
